To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the stereospecific fluorination of a ligand, (-)-balanol (a non-natural ATP mimic) uncovers a new mechanism for differentiating homologous sites.

1) the homologous ATP binding sites of protein kinase C (PKC) and protein kinase A (PKA) have different responses to stereospecific fluorination of the ligand; 2) the PKC homodimer is stabilized by the ligand fluorination, while the PKA homodimer is destabilized; 3) the conformational response of the ligand is the primary source of selectivity; 4) the ligand conformational response
stereospecific fluorination of balanol, an ATP mimetic, differentiates homologues ATP sites in protein kinases by the level of response to local and distant fluorine effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of new, selective inhibitors of protein-protein and protein-nucleic acid interactions, which are of fundamental interest and of potential therapeutic value.
the design and synthesis of novel ligands that can selectively bind to a target protein, and the development of new methods for the synthesis of complex organic molecules.
the development and application of novel fluorine chemistry to the design of selective protein-ligand interactions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fluorination of the C2 position of (-)-balanal is a powerful tool for the design of selective inhibitors for the PDE4D5 and PDE4B2 isoforms of PDE4.
the fluorine effect on ATP binding is site-specific and dependent upon the local protein environment.
the stereospecific fluorine effects on ligand binding and conformational change are not the same in all cases, and that these effects are not additive, as they are in some cases, and not in others.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how a subtle chemical modification can lead to a significant difference in the response of homologues sites to the same ligand.
we have identified a new source of ligand selectivity that is dependent on the level of homology between protein sites.
the homologous sites of the protein domains have a divergent response to stereospecific fluorination.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fluorine can provide a powerful means to modulate ligand-protein recognition by exploiting the differential response to local and long-range fluorine effects.
the divergent response of homologic protein sites to stereospecified ligand fluorination can be exploited for the design of highly selective ligands.
a small chemical perturbation can be leveraged to generate selectivity by exploiting a differential response from homologously related proteins.
